new.title: Cross Pegasus Bridge where D-Day began
new.desc: Bénouville Bridge over the Caen Canal was captured by glider-borne British troops under Major John Howard in the first minutes of 6 June 1944 and renamed Pegasus Bridge. The original 1935 bridge now stands in the grounds of the Mémorial Pegasus, while its modern replacement spans the canal.
new.tip: The bridge and the original span can be seen free at any time. The Mémorial Pegasus museum is announced as closed for renovation from 31 August 2026 to May 2027, so check before planning a museum visit.
new.q: Pegasus Bridge, Avenue du Major Howard, Bénouville

new.title: Climb the German fire-control tower at Le Grand Bunker
new.desc: Le Grand Bunker is a five-level German fire-control tower in Ouistreham, part of the Atlantic Wall battery behind Sword Beach. Allied troops took it on 9 June 1944 and captured 53 German soldiers. Its rooms are restored with command post equipment and period objects.
new.tip: Allow about 45 minutes. It is a short walk from the beach and the ferry terminal, and opening hours change with the season.
new.q: Musée du Grand Bunker, Avenue du 6 Juin, Ouistreham

new.title: Learn the Canadian D-Day story at the Juno Beach Centre
new.desc: The Juno Beach Centre in Courseulles-sur-Mer was built by veterans and opened on 6 June 2003 directly behind the beach where Canadian troops landed. Exhibits cover Canada in the Second World War and modern Canada, and young Canadian guides lead tours of the preserved Atlantic Wall bunker.
new.tip: The centre is closed in January and hours vary by season. Book the guided bunker tour when you buy your ticket.
new.q: Juno Beach Centre, Voie des Français Libres, Courseulles-sur-Mer

new.title: See the Mulberry harbour from the Musée du Débarquement
new.desc: The Musée du Débarquement in Arromanches opened in 1954 and is often called the first museum devoted to D-Day. It faces the remains of Mulberry B, the artificial harbour assembled here in June 1944, and has an animated model of how it was built. The museum was renovated and reopened in 2023.
new.tip: Go on to the rooftop terrace for the view of the caissons. At low tide you can walk down to the nearest remains on the beach.
new.q: Musée du Débarquement, Place du 6 Juin, Arromanches-les-Bains

new.title: Stand beside the original guns at Longues-sur-Mer
new.desc: The Longues-sur-Mer battery (Wn 48) was built from September 1943 and had four 150 mm naval guns in concrete casemates. It is the only Normandy battery on the coast that still has its original guns. Allied ships, including HMS Ajax, silenced it on D-Day and it was captured on 7 June 1944.
new.tip: The site is outdoors and open to visitors year round. Allow an hour and combine it with the clifftop views toward Arromanches.
new.q: Batterie de Longues-sur-Mer, Longues-sur-Mer

new.title: Pay respects at the Normandy American Cemetery
new.desc: The cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer overlooks Omaha Beach and holds about 9,380 American war dead, most killed in the Normandy campaign of 1944. The visitor center, dedicated on 6 June 2007, shows exhibits and three films on Operation Overlord.
new.tip: Entry and parking are free and the site is open every day. Allow at least two hours and go early in summer to avoid coach crowds.
new.q: Cimetière américain de Normandie, Colleville-sur-Mer

new.title: Walk the shell craters of Pointe du Hoc
new.desc: Pointe du Hoc is a clifftop German gun position that the US 2nd Ranger Battalion scaled on 6 June 1944; only 90 of the 225 Rangers survived the assault. The American Battle Monuments Commission has maintained it since 1979, and the bomb craters and bunkers are preserved.
new.tip: Entry is free and the site is open daily (typically 9 am to 5 pm, 6 pm in summer). Stay on the marked paths because the cliff edge is eroded.
new.q: Pointe du Hoc, Cricqueville-en-Bessin

new.title: Admire Notre-Dame de Bayeux cathedral
new.desc: Bayeux Cathedral was dedicated on 14 July 1077 in the presence of William the Conqueror and mixes Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The Bayeux Tapestry was long kept here, and the crossing tower was finished only in the 19th century.
new.tip: Entry is free. Walk around the east end and the Romanesque crypt, and look for the Norman arches in the nave.
new.q: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Bayeux, Rue du Bienvenu, Bayeux

new.title: Follow the Battle of Normandy at the Bayeux memorial museum
new.desc: The Musée Mémorial de la Bataille de Normandie covers the fighting from 7 June to 29 August 1944 across 2,000 square metres, with dioramas, vehicles, photographs and civilian testimony. It stands opposite the British military cemetery on Boulevard Fabian Ware.
new.tip: Expect around two hours. Combine it with the British cemetery across the road, which is free and has the Bayeux Memorial.
new.q: Musée Mémorial de la Bataille de Normandie, Boulevard Fabian Ware, Bayeux

new.title: Photograph the Vieux Bassin from La Lieutenance
new.desc: The Vieux Bassin in Honfleur was dug in 1681 on Colbert's orders. La Lieutenance at its mouth is the last remnant of the town fortifications and the former home of the royal lieutenant. It was classified as a historic monument in 1909 and now holds a maritime history centre.
new.tip: The facade and the quay are free to see at any time. Hours of the interpretation centre vary, so check with the tourist office.
new.q: La Lieutenance, Quai de la Planchette, Honfleur

new.title: Step inside Honfleur's wooden Église Sainte-Catherine
new.desc: Sainte-Catherine was built in the late 15th and early 16th centuries by local shipwrights, who gave its twin naves the look of upturned hulls. It is one of France's largest wooden churches and its bell tower stands separately across the square. It was classified as a historic monument in 1875.
new.tip: Entry is free. Visit in the morning, before the Saturday market stalls fill the square outside.
new.q: Église Sainte-Catherine, Place Sainte-Catherine, Honfleur

new.title: Visit the Basilica of Sainte-Thérèse in Lisieux
new.desc: The neo-Byzantine basilica was begun in 1929 and consecrated in 1954. It is the second most visited pilgrimage site in France after Lourdes and holds relics of Saint Thérèse. The crypt holds the shrine of her parents Louis and Zélie Martin.
new.tip: Admission is free. Daily hours run roughly 9:30 to 18:00, so check the schedule on the day of your visit.
new.q: Basilique Sainte-Thérèse, Avenue Sainte-Thérèse, Lisieux

new.title: Explore Falaise castle, birthplace of William the Conqueror
new.desc: Château de Falaise is the Norman fortress where William the Conqueror was born around 1028. It has a Romanesque keep and the tall round Talbot Tower, which dates from the early 13th century and was repaired by the English governor Talbot. It has been a historic monument since 1840.
new.tip: The audioguide and the old guardrooms tell the story of William. Park below the castle and walk up through the old town.
new.q: Château Guillaume-le-Conquérant, Place Guillaume le Conquérant, Falaise

new.title: Stroll the half-timbered village of Beuvron-en-Auge
new.desc: Beuvron-en-Auge is the only village in Calvados with the Plus Beaux Villages de France label. Its 16th to 18th century half-timbered houses surround a central market hall restored in 1975 using old materials. The 17th-century inn La Boule d'Or stands on the square.
new.tip: Visit mid-morning and combine it with the nearby cider and calvados producers of the Route du Cidre.
new.q: Place du Marché, Beuvron-en-Auge

new.title: Tour the Château de Saint-Germain-de-Livet
new.desc: This chequerboard stone-and-flint château in the Pays d'Auge was built by the Tournebu family between 1561 and 1578 on the site of an older fortress. The city of Lisieux received it by donation in the 1950s and runs it as a château-museum.
new.tip: The park is free and the interior is visited on guided tours, from April to the first weekend of November. It is a short drive south of Lisieux.
new.q: Château de Saint-Germain-de-Livet, Saint-Germain-de-Livet

new.title: Walk the Planches boardwalk past the Deauville beach cabins
new.desc: Les Planches is Deauville's promenade, built in 1923 along the Bains Pompéiens, with about 450 Art Deco beach cabins, many named after stars of the American Film Festival. The boardwalk is a listed monument and is lit at night.
new.tip: Walking it is free. Start at the Casino end at sunset, and note that renting a cabin has to be booked far ahead.
new.q: Les Planches, Boulevard de la Mer, Deauville

new.title: See the Porte-Horloge gate in Vire
new.desc: The Porte-Horloge in Vire is a 13th-century town gate, once called Porte Gastinel, that was raised to 33 metres when a belfry with a clock and bell was added in 1499. It was listed as a historic monument in 1886 and hosts exhibitions.
new.tip: Nearby, the ruined donjon of the ducal castle sits on a rock above the Vire valley. The tourist office is a short walk away.
new.q: Porte-Horloge, Rue Chaussée, Vire-Normandie

new.title: Taste aged calvados at Christian Drouin
new.desc: Calvados Christian Drouin in Coudray-Rabut offers a free guided visit of its press, distillery and ageing cellars. It ends with a tasting of pommeau, cider, calvados and gin, and the house holds more than 35 vintages back to 1939.
new.tip: The tour lasts about an hour. Phone ahead on 02 31 64 30 05 in low season and ask for a vintage calvados at the end.
new.q: Calvados Christian Drouin, Route de Trouville, Coudray-Rabut

new.title: Sip Pays d'Auge calvados at Château du Breuil
new.desc: Château du Breuil in Le Breuil-en-Auge is a calvados estate that offers distillery and ageing-cellar visits. Tastings run from the Réserve du Château to 8, 12, 15 and 20-year-old Pays d'Auge calvados and Pommeau de Normandie.
new.tip: Prices and formats vary, from a short visit to a longer private tour, so book through the estate. Try the 12-year-old.
new.q: Château du Breuil, Les Jourdains, Le Breuil-en-Auge

new.title: Taste cider, pommeau and calvados at Pierre Huet
new.desc: The Pierre Huet estate in Cambremer produces cider, Pommeau AOC and Calvados Pays d'Auge. A guided tour of the estate ends with a tasting of the three products, with juice for children and non-drinkers.
new.tip: The visit takes about 75 minutes and is closed on Sundays in low season. Ask for the Cambremer cider with a bottle of pommeau to take home.
new.q: Calvados Pierre Huet, Avenue des Tilleuls, Cambremer

new.title: Taste Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque at Fromagerie Graindorge
new.desc: The Village Fromager of Fromagerie Graindorge in Livarot is a free self-guided visit through glass galleries showing how Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque cheeses are made. A small museum covers Norman dairy history. The visit ends with a tasting of the Norman cheeses.
new.tip: Go in the morning, not on Friday, and allow about 90 minutes. The last visit starts at 16:00.
new.q: Fromagerie Graindorge, Rue du Général Leclerc, Livarot

new.title: Eat fresh seafood at the Trouville fish market
new.desc: The 1930s neo-Norman Halle aux Poissons on the Touques quay in Trouville is a listed building where stalls sell the day's catch. Pillet-Saiter is a well-known fishmonger in the hall that also sells shellfish for eating on the spot.
new.tip: Buy a plate of shrimp or oysters and eat on the quay. Stalls generally open from 8 am and Pillet-Saiter lists daily hours.
new.q: Poissonnerie Pillet-Saiter, Boulevard Fernand Moureaux, Trouville-sur-Mer

new.title: Try tarte normande at À la Reine Mathilde in Bayeux
new.desc: À la Reine Mathilde is a pâtisserie, chocolate shop and tea room on rue Saint-Martin, founded in 1898. Guests mention its tarte normande with apples and the Paris-Brest.
new.tip: Take a slice of tarte normande to the cathedral gardens. The shop is a few minutes from the cathedral.
new.q: À la Reine Mathilde, 47 Rue Saint-Martin, Bayeux

new.title: Watch and taste Isigny caramels in Isigny-sur-Mer
new.desc: The Caramels d'Isigny visitor area lets you see salted-butter caramels made, with an immersive walk through Isigny's dairy specialities and tastings. It sits beside the Isigny Sainte-Mère cooperative, which produces the AOP butter and cream.
new.tip: The visit takes about 45 minutes; there is a small entry fee. Buy the salted-butter caramels in the shop at the end.
new.q: Caramels d'Isigny, Zone Isypôle, Isigny-sur-Mer

new.title: Order a soufflé at Chez Miocque in Deauville
new.desc: Chez Miocque is a long-standing Deauville restaurant on rue Eugène-Colas that reopened under new owners at the end of 2025. Its desserts include a soufflé au Cointreau and a tarte fine aux pommes flambée au Calvados.
new.tip: Weekday lunch menus are the cheapest way in. Book ahead in race and festival weeks.
new.q: Chez Miocque, 81 Rue Eugène Colas, Deauville

new.title: Dine on modern Norman cuisine at Le Bréard in Honfleur
new.desc: Le Bréard on rue du Puits is a Michelin-guide listed restaurant serving creative contemporary French cooking in the old town, within walking distance of the Vieux Bassin.
new.tip: Reservations are advisable, especially at weekends. Ask which seafood is local that day.
new.q: Le Bréard, 7 Rue du Puits, Honfleur

new.title: Taste true andouille de Vire at Maison Asselot
new.desc: Maison Asselot is an andouillerie in Vire founded in 1981 by Lucien Asselot, making traditional andouille de Vire. The sausage is made of pork stomach and intestines and gets its black colour from smoking, with no colouring allowed.
new.tip: Slice it cold as a starter or grill it. Vire also holds an annual andouille fair, the Foire à l'Andouille.
new.q: Andouilles Asselot, rue de l'Allière, Vire Normandie

new.title: Slurp oysters at Dégustation de l'Île in Courseulles
new.desc: The Benoist family has farmed oysters in Courseulles-sur-Mer since the 1950s and runs the restaurant Dégustation de l'Île beside the beds. The port's last oyster park lies on the Île de Plaisance, and Courseulles oysters are a local speciality.
new.tip: Order a dozen with white wine, then walk the harbour. Opening varies by season, so check before going.
new.q: Dégustation de l'Île, Route de Ver-sur-Mer, Courseulles-sur-Mer

new.title: Try Caen-style tripe at Le Pommier in Bayeux
new.desc: Le Pommier is a restaurant in an old stone building in Bayeux serving traditional Norman dishes with a modern twist, including steamed pollock and tripe in the Caen style. It also offers a vegetarian menu.
new.tip: Book for dinner in summer. Order the Caen-style tripe if you want a local classic.
new.q: Le Pommier, Rue Saint-Martin, Bayeux

new.title: Hike the Pain de Sucre and Rochers des Parcs from Clécy
new.desc: Loop trails from Clécy climb to the Pain de Sucre and the Rochers des Parcs, climbing cliffs above a meander of the Orne in the Suisse Normande. Routes run roughly 7 to 10 km with up to 250 m or more of climbing, with views of the Clécy viaduct.
new.tip: Start from Clécy village. Wear walking shoes because the rock paths are steep and slippery after rain.
new.q: Pain de Sucre, Clécy

new.title: Paddle the Orne from Pont-d'Ouilly to Clécy
new.desc: Pont d'Ouilly Loisirs rents canoes, kayaks and stand-up paddles at the launch ramp in Pont-d'Ouilly. A 13 km descent runs to Clécy, and a shorter 5 km trip ends at the Moulin Neuf weir.
new.tip: Kayaking is open to anyone aged 8 and over who can swim. Book in summer and confirm the opening season with the base.
new.q: Pont d'Ouilly Loisirs, Pont-d'Ouilly

new.title: Walk the Vaches Noires cliffs from Houlgate
new.desc: The Falaises des Vaches Noires between Houlgate and Villers-sur-Mer are fossil-rich clay cliffs where ammonites, urchins and corals have been found. The beach route is about 7 km and is only passable at low tide.
new.tip: Check tide times first. Guided fossil walks are run by the Paléospace in Villers-sur-Mer.
new.q: Falaises des Vaches Noires, Houlgate

new.title: Browse the Saturday market around Honfleur's Sainte-Catherine
new.desc: Honfleur's traditional market spreads around the Église Sainte-Catherine, selling Norman cheeses, charcuterie, seafood and produce. An organic market is held on Wednesday mornings on the same square.
new.tip: Go on Saturday between about 8:30 and 13:00 and check the tourist office for changes.
new.q: Place Sainte-Catherine, Honfleur

new.title: Join the Deauville American Film Festival
new.desc: The Festival du cinéma américain de Deauville has been held since 1975. Its 52nd edition ran from 4 to 13 September 2026, with screenings at the CID, the Casino cinema and the Morny cinema.
new.tip: Ticket sales open on the festival website. Early September falls on the first race week, so book rooms early.
new.q: Centre International de Deauville (CID), Avenue Lucien Barrière, Deauville

new.title: Shop the Saturday market at Place Saint-Patrice, Bayeux
new.desc: Place Saint-Patrice holds Bayeux's largest outdoor market on Saturday mornings, with local produce, street food, plants and animals. The square has hosted a market since Roman times.
new.tip: Get there before 10 am for the best choice. A separate flea market also uses the square on other dates.
new.q: Place Saint-Patrice, Bayeux

new.title: Stroll the Promenade Marcel Proust and swim at Cabourg
new.desc: Cabourg's beachfront promenade, named after Marcel Proust, runs about 3.6 km along a wide sandy beach in front of the Grand Hôtel, which inspired Balbec in his novel. The beach shelves gently, with lifeguards in season.
new.tip: The tide returns fast, so follow the flags. Kitesurfing and paddle are common here.
new.q: Promenade Marcel Proust, Cabourg

new.title: Cruise the Seine estuary from Honfleur to the Pont de Normandie
new.desc: Roney Boats runs a 90-minute guided trip aboard the Ville d'Honfleur into the estuary and beneath the Pont de Normandie, plus a shorter 45-minute harbour trip. The Bateau Aventura offers a 1h30 sea cruise with live commentary.
new.tip: Prices are about 19 to 20 euros per adult. Check times with the operator.
new.q: Roney Boats, Voie Charles Berthelot, Honfleur

new.title: Walk the Mont Canisy batteries above Bénerville
new.desc: Mont Canisy is a wooded headland above Bénerville-sur-Mer with the remains of German coastal batteries and bunkers. A signed nature trail is about 2.4 km, while longer loops link Blonville and Villers-sur-Mer with sea views.
new.tip: Paths can be muddy. The short nature trail takes about 40 minutes.
new.q: Mont Canisy, Bénerville-sur-Mer

new.title: Cycle the Route du Cidre loop from Cambremer
new.desc: The Route du Cidre is a roughly 40 km loop linking Cambremer, Beuvron-en-Auge, Bonnebosq and Beaufour-Druval, with stops at Cru Cambremer cider producers. Shorter Komoot loops of about 19 km are also available.
new.tip: E-bikes can be rented in Lisieux or Pont-l'Évêque, so reserve in summer. Plan stops at two producers only.
new.q: Cambremer, Route du Cidre

new.title: Taste scallops at Le Goût du Large in Port-en-Bessin
new.desc: Port-en-Bessin-Huppain is Normandy's top port by landed tonnage and first in France for scallops. The Goût du Large festival opens the fish auction hall to visitors for a scallop weekend, with tastings, chef workshops and meetings with fishermen. The 2026 edition was listed for 7 to 8 November.
new.tip: The scallop season runs October to May. Confirm the next dates with the port.
new.q: Criée de Port-en-Bessin, Quai Baron Gérard, Port-en-Bessin-Huppain

new.title: Watch films on the beach at the Cabourg Film Festival
new.desc: The Festival du Film de Cabourg, founded in 1986 by Gonzague Saint-Bris, screens romantic films in local cinemas and outdoors on the beach below the Grand Hôtel. The 40th edition ran from 10 to 14 June 2026.
new.tip: It takes place each year in mid-June. Book rooms well ahead.
new.q: Festival du Film de Cabourg, Avenue de la Mer, Cabourg

new.title: Walk Omaha Beach from the Vierville draw
new.desc: Vierville-sur-Mer is at the west end of Omaha Beach. The National Guard Monument stands on German strongpoint WN72 and other memorials sit within a few metres. A loop of about 6 km on Komoot starts from Vierville.
new.tip: Parking is easier at the memorials than in the village. Allow time to walk to the Musée Mémorial d'Omaha Beach at Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer.
new.q: National Guard Monument, Vierville-sur-Mer
